opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is that compositionality is what lets the whole wake-sleep loop actually bootstrap itself rather than just spin its wheels.

Think about what's going on in something like DreamCoder. During the wake phase, you're trying to solve tasks by searching for programs, and that search is exponentially hard in the length of the program. So the only way you get traction on harder problems is if the programs you need become *shorter* over time. And compositionality is exactly what buys you that. When you notice that some chunk of code keeps showing up across a bunch of solutions, you can abstract it out into a new library primitive, and now everything that uses it gets shorter. Programs that were out of reach become reachable. That's the abstraction or "sleep-abstraction" phase, and it only works because programs are built out of reusable parts that can be pulled apart and recombined.

Then there's the dreaming phase, where you train a neural recognition model on fantasies: you sample programs from your current library, run them, and get synthetic input-output pairs to learn from. Compositionality matters a lot there too, because when you sample from a compositional generative model you get an essentially unbounded and structured space of examples. You're not just replaying what you've seen; you're recombining learned concepts in new ways, and that gives the neural network a much richer curriculum than the handful of real tasks you started with.

And the neat thing is these feed into each other. Better abstractions make search easier and make dreams more meaningful; better recognition models solve more tasks; more solved tasks give you more evidence for what's worth abstracting. It's a virtuous cycle, but it hinges on the representation being compositional. If you had some opaque, monolithic representation, there'd be nothing to factor out, nothing to reuse, and nothing to recombine.

There's also a more philosophical angle I care about, which is that compositionality is how humans seem to get such strong generalization from little data. We build up a vocabulary of concepts and then express new ideas by composing them. Programs give you a really clean, explicit way of modeling that: the knowledge is interpretable, it's symbolic, and you can inspect what the system has learned. You can look at the library and say, oh, it invented something like a "map" function, or a routine for drawing a radial pattern. So compositional programs aren't just an engineering convenience for wake-sleep; they're kind of the right inductive bias for the kind of cumulative, open-ended learning we want these systems to do.

r002.rationale: It says compositional sampling recombines learned concepts in new ways, generating a structured space of examples beyond those previously seen.

r003.rationale: It says dreams should provide a richer curriculum than the original real tasks by recombining learned concepts in new ways.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is that compositional programs are what make the sleep phase actually pay off.

Think about what wake-sleep is doing. In the wake phase you have some generative model and you're trying to explain observed data by inferring latent structure for it. In the sleep phase you sample from the generative model, which gives you data where you know the latent cause by construction, and you train a recognition network on those pairs so that next time inference is fast. The whole thing hinges on the dreams being useful. If your sampled fantasies are nonsense, or they're just regurgitations of the handful of things you've already solved, the recognition model learns nothing new.

Programs fix that because they compose. If you've learned a few primitives, or in DreamCoder's case a few library abstractions, and you sample programs that combine them, you get a combinatorial explosion of new tasks that are structurally related to the ones you've seen but not identical. The recognition model is trained on that whole space, so it generalizes to problems it's never encountered, because they're built from the same parts.

There's also a nice feedback loop. The abstraction step compresses solutions from the wake phase into reusable library components. That makes the library richer, which makes the dreams richer, which makes the recognition model better, which means in the next wake phase you can solve harder problems in the search budget you have. Every cycle, the programs you can express concisely grow, and so does the data you can hallucinate for free. You don't get that with an unstructured latent space, because sampling from it doesn't produce anything with that kind of systematic, reusable structure.

r001.rationale: The response describes a compression-and-expansion feedback loop in wake-sleep learning, but does not identify it as a general pattern in intelligent systems.

r002.rationale: It explains that learned primitives or library abstractions can be combined into many new, structurally related tasks that were not previously encountered.

r003.rationale: It says sampled dreams should be structurally related to known tasks but not identical, creating useful training examples beyond waking experience.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that compositional programs give you a way to reuse what you’ve learned. You can discover a solution to one problem, extract a useful subroutine, and then use that subroutine as a building block for solving other problems. So learning changes the space in which you search, rather than just giving you another isolated solution.

That fits very naturally with wake-sleep learning. During wake, you’re trying to find programs that explain the tasks you actually encounter. Then you can look across those programs and discover shared structure—a library of useful abstractions. During sleep, you can sample programs from that library, generate synthetic tasks, and train a recognition model to predict which programs are likely to solve which tasks.

The compositionality is what makes those imagined examples interesting: you can recombine familiar pieces in new ways. And that gives you a feedback loop. Better abstractions make useful programs easier to express and discover; better recognition makes the search faster; and finding more programs gives you more material from which to learn abstractions.

r003.rationale: It mentions generating synthetic tasks and recombining pieces, but does not clearly argue that dreams should extend somewhat beyond waking experience.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a compositional program gives you a way to represent a lot of different behaviors using a relatively small set of reusable pieces. And that’s useful for wake-sleep learning because what you learn on one problem can help you solve another problem with a different combination of those pieces.

In the wake phase, you’re trying to find programs that explain the tasks you’ve actually observed. Then, in the sleep phase, you can sample programs and generate synthetic tasks, and use those to train a recognition model that helps you search for programs more efficiently. So you have this loop: solving tasks improves your model of programs, and dreaming up programs improves your ability to solve tasks.

Compositionality makes that loop particularly powerful because you don’t have to encounter every possible task. You can learn useful components and practice putting them together, and hopefully generalize to combinations you haven’t seen before.

r002.rationale: It says learned components can be put together in combinations not seen before, communicating that compositionality supports unseen combinations of learned pieces.

r003.rationale: It says the sleep phase samples programs to generate synthetic tasks and practice combinations that have not been encountered, so dreaming extends beyond observed waking tasks.
